messages.subject: Input model for Distance Sampling
parts:
Hello team distance sampling,


I am currently analyzing data for 1 group of gibbon in Vietnam after 2 years of monitoring (2020 and 2022). However, I am not used to applying the distance method for combining data for 2 years, to calculate population density data.

I currently have 2-year ape observation distance data at 12 observation points. I ran on version 7.5 of 2 years combined. 

The results of the monitoring after the estimate are equal to the actual results of the field. I'm not sure if it's correct for me to merge the template to run the same on 1 time? Or do I need to separate each year's data for separate calculations?

Sample data recorded relatively small ape colonies with n = 6 group (2020) and n = 8 group(2022). With the results of the collection monitoring efforts, will there be any impact on the input data for the model?

Best regards,

 Tay.

messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Input model for Distance Sampling
parts:
Tay

Thanks for the screenshot. You have organised your data in such a manner that you are using year as a strata, which is fine. The software will produce stratum-specific estimates of abundance.

The portion of the analysis you need to consider is whether the detection function is the same for each year. To determine this, you should fit a model with a pooled detection function and contrast with a model with a stratum-specific detection function.  The way you do this with Distance for Windows is shown below:

Pooled detection function:

Year-specific detection function:


Comparison of AIC scores will help you assess which modelling approach is appropriate.

I should mention that the data shown in your screen shot is very meagre. Six and eight year-specific detections are insufficient to fit detection functions. If the screen shot is merely a subset of your data, that's fine; but if it is the totality of your data, then you are likely to be unable to fit a detection function. Is that why you said
The results of the monitoring after the estimate are equal to the actual results of the field.

This would be the outcome if a flat (horizontal) detection function resulted from analysis of these data (which seems quite likely). In that case, detection probability is predicted to be perfect and the estimated abundance is equal to the number of detections. That seems unlikely to be the reality (in a 100 km^2 study area) and is the result of a small number of detections.

Correct me if I have misunderstood your questions.
